scene-u01.name: Pattern Recognition Week 3 KP06 Kesler Construction (expert-first, English)

p01-regions-title.name: p01-regions-title
p01-regions-title.text: Three classes: the sample goes to whichever has the highest score

p01-regions-ctx.name: p01-regions-ctx
p01-regions-ctx.text: Each class $i$ has its own score $g_i=\mathbf w_i^T\mathbf a$. For one sample, put the three scores side by side; the highest is the predicted class.

p01-regions-src.name: p01-regions-src
p01-regions-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture §1 and Example 3.3 (9 samples, 3 sets of weights); the background colors are the highest-score regions computed from the given weights, no retraining.

p01-regions-c0.name: p01-regions-c0
p01-regions-c0.text: Each class has a set of weights $\mathbf w_i$. Compute three scores at every point of the plane and assign the point to the highest. What do the three highest-score regions look like?

p01-regions-cr0.name: p01-regions-cr0
p01-regions-cr0.text: ω₁'s highest-score region: $g_1>g_2$ and $g_1>g_3$. All three blue circles are inside.

p01-regions-cr1.name: p01-regions-cr1
p01-regions-cr1.text: ω₂'s highest-score region: $g_2>g_1$ and $g_2>g_3$. All three red triangles are inside.

p01-regions-cr2.name: p01-regions-cr2
p01-regions-cr2.text: ω₃'s highest-score region: $g_3>g_1$ and $g_3>g_2$. All three green squares are inside.

p01-regions-c4.name: p01-regions-c4
p01-regions-c4.text: The three regions cover the plane. Note: the region boundaries are lines where "two scores are equal", not three unrelated lines.

p02-beat-all-title.name: p02-beat-all-title
p02-beat-all-title.text: "Highest score" means beating every rival at once; beating one is not enough

p02-beat-all-ctx.name: p02-beat-all-ctx
p02-beat-all-ctx.text: A sample of class $i$ must satisfy $g_i>g_j$ for every $j\ne i$. In training a tie also counts as not winning.

p02-beat-all-src.name: p02-beat-all-src
p02-beat-all-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture §1 "formal definition"; the scores of sample $(1,1)$ come from Example 3.3, and the second set of scores $(2.0,2.5,1.0)$ is a contrast added on this page.

p02-beat-all-c0.name: p02-beat-all-c0
p02-beat-all-c0.text: See the left first: is ω₁'s score the highest? How many rivals must it beat?

p02-beat-all-c1.name: p02-beat-all-c1
p02-beat-all-c1.text: Beats ω₂: $g_1-g_2=13.35>0$; beats ω₃: $g_1-g_3=11.6>0$. Winning both makes ω₁ the highest.

p02-beat-all-hb.name: p02-beat-all-hb
p02-beat-all-hb.text: Another sample (true class ω₁, hypothetical scores)

p02-beat-all-c2.name: p02-beat-all-c2
p02-beat-all-c2.text: $g_1=2.0$ beats $g_3=1.0$ but loses to $g_2=2.5$. Beating only one is not the highest score: $g_1>g_2$ fails, so this sample is not classified correctly.

p02-beat-all-c3.name: p02-beat-all-c3
p02-beat-all-c3.text: So a sample must satisfy $M-1$ constraints (one comparison with each rival). Training constraints are strict $>0$: a tie $g_i=g_j$ also counts as "not yet won". Only prediction may use a separate tie rule.

p03-blocks-title.name: p03-blocks-title
p03-blocks-title.text: Write the difference of two scores as one inner product: the Kesler block vector

p03-blocks-ctx.name: p03-blocks-ctx
p03-blocks-ctx.text: Concatenate the three classes' weights into one long vector $\mathbf v=(\mathbf w_1,\mathbf w_2,\mathbf w_3)$ (9 numbers). With a $\mathbf z_{ij}$ of the same length, the inner product is $g_i-g_j$.

p03-blocks-src.name: p03-blocks-src
p03-blocks-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture §2: $\mathbf z_{12}=(\mathbf a,-\mathbf a,\mathbf 0)$, $\mathbf z_{13}=(\mathbf a,\mathbf 0,-\mathbf a)$; the sample $\mathbf a=(1,1,1)$ and the weights come from Example 3.3.

p03-blocks-c0.name: p03-blocks-c0
p03-blocks-c0.text: Each of the three rows has 9 numbers in three blocks. The first row is the weights; the second and third are "comparison vectors". What are the blocks in rows two and three?

p03-blocks-c1.name: p03-blocks-c1
p03-blocks-c1.text: Block-wise inner product: $\mathbf v^T\mathbf z_{12}=\mathbf w_1^T\mathbf a-\mathbf w_2^T\mathbf a+0=9.73-(-3.62)=13.35$. The zero block contributes nothing.

p03-blocks-c2.name: p03-blocks-c2
p03-blocks-c2.text: Likewise: $\mathbf v^T\mathbf z_{13}=9.73-(-1.87)=11.6>0$. Every comparison is one "positive inner product" constraint.

p03-blocks-c3.name: p03-blocks-c3
p03-blocks-c3.text: With $N$ samples, $M$ classes and $l$ raw features: $N(M-1)$ vectors in all, each of length $M(l+1)$. Here $l=2$: each has length $9$.

p04-check-title.name: p04-check-title
p04-check-title.text: Nine samples, eighteen constraints: does the given weight set satisfy all? Which is the tightest?

p04-check-ctx.name: p04-check-ctx
p04-check-ctx.text: Each sample is compared once with each of its two rivals, giving $9\times2=18$ constraints $\mathbf v^T\mathbf z_{ij}>0$. Plot them on a number line to see where they fall.

p04-check-src.name: p04-check-src
p04-check-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture Example 3.3 and [supplement] (Python check, minimum 0.17); the 18 values are recomputed by build_kp06_en.py and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp06.py.

p04-check-c0.name: p04-check-c0
p04-check-c0.text: All 18 constraint values $g_i-g_j$ (the correct class's score minus the rival's) must exceed 0. See the two for sample $(1,1)$ first, then all.

p04-check-c2.name: p04-check-c2
p04-check-c2.text: The tightest constraint: the ω₂ sample $(1,-1)$ against ω₁: $g_2-g_1=2.70-2.53=0.17$. Still above 0 but very close.

p04-check-c3.name: p04-check-c3
p04-check-c3.text: All 18 constraints lie between $0.17$ and $25.29$ (green band); none is at or below 0: the given $\mathbf v$ is feasible, and every sample's highest score is its own class.

p05-update-title.name: p05-update-title
p05-update-title.text: Fixing a failing constraint: add z_ij to v, the correct class's score rises and the rival's falls

p05-update-ctx.name: p05-update-ctx
p05-update-ctx.text: Start from $\mathbf w_1=\mathbf w_2=\mathbf w_3=\mathbf 0$ with learning rate $\rho=0.5$, sample $(1,1)$ (ω₁). Update $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v+\rho\mathbf z_{ij}$.

p05-update-src.name: p05-update-src
p05-update-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture §2 update rule (equivalently: add $\rho\mathbf a$ to the correct class, subtract $\rho\mathbf a$ from the rival); the start $\mathbf 0$ and $\rho=0.5$ are this page's teaching example, numbers computed by build_kp06_en.py.

p05-update-c0.name: p05-update-c0
p05-update-c0.text: The start is all 0: both constraints $g_1-g_2=0$ and $g_1-g_3=0$ fail (a tie is not a win). Fix them one by one and watch the three scores.

p05-update-c1.name: p05-update-c1
p05-update-c1.text: Fix $\mathbf z_{12}$: $\mathbf w_1\leftarrow\mathbf w_1+0.5\mathbf a$, $\mathbf w_2\leftarrow\mathbf w_2-0.5\mathbf a$. Then $g_1=1.5$, $g_2=-1.5$.

p05-update-c2.name: p05-update-c2
p05-update-c2.text: Fix $\mathbf z_{13}$: add to $\mathbf w_1$ again, subtract from $\mathbf w_3$. Then $g_1=3$, $g_3=-1.5$, $g_2$ unchanged.

p05-update-c3.name: p05-update-c3
p05-update-c3.text: Check: $g_1-g_2=4.5>0$, $g_1-g_3=4.5>0$, both constraints hold. Each fix touches only two non-zero blocks: no need to actually build the long zero vector.

p06-limits-title.name: p06-limits-title
p06-limits-title.text: Adding the same vector to every class does not change the score differences: the feasible solution is not unique

p06-limits-ctx.name: p06-limits-ctx
p06-limits-ctx.text: Add $\mathbf u=(1,1,1)$ to all of $\mathbf w_1,\mathbf w_2,\mathbf w_3$. What happens to the three scores and the two differences of sample $(1,1)$?

p06-limits-src.name: p06-limits-src
p06-limits-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture §4 [going deeper] and "common myths"; $\mathbf u=(1,1,1)$ is this page's example, computed by build_kp06_en.py.

p06-limits-c0.name: p06-limits-c0
p06-limits-c0.text: If every class's weights get the same vector added, who rises? Whose rank changes? Guess first.

p06-limits-tb.name: p06-limits-tb
p06-limits-tb.text: After adding $\mathbf u=(1,1,1)$ to each class

p06-limits-c1.name: p06-limits-c1
p06-limits-c1.text: All three scores gained the same number $\mathbf u^T\mathbf a=3$: they become $12.73,-0.62,1.13$. The ranking is unchanged; ω₁ is still the highest.

p06-limits-c2.name: p06-limits-c2
p06-limits-c2.text: Both differences are unchanged: $g_1-g_2=13.35$, $g_1-g_3=11.6$. So feasible weights are not unique: as long as the differences stay, a whole family of solutions exists.

p06-limits-c3.name: p06-limits-c3
p06-limits-c3.text: Three reminders: (1) Kesler only rewrites the linear-score constraints in a single form; it does not make non-separable data separable; (2) it is not "one versus rest": all comparisons share one set of class weights; (3) finite-step convergence still requires the constraints to have a strictly feasible solution.

p06-limits-c4.name: p06-limits-c4
p06-limits-c4.text: In practice you need not build the $M(l+1)$-dimensional zero vector; update only the two non-zero blocks each time.

p07-practice-title.name: p07-practice-title
p07-practice-title.text: Practice: 4 classes, 5 features: how long is the vector? What do scores (2.4, 2.1, 2.3) give?

p07-practice-ctx.name: p07-practice-ctx
p07-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: include the bias position first ($l+1$), then multiply by the number of classes; a constraint is "the correct class's score" minus "each rival". Press Next when done.

p07-practice-src.name: p07-practice-src
p07-practice-src.text: Source: KP06 lecture practice ($M=4,l=5$; $g_1=2.4,g_2=2.1,g_3=2.3$); answer computed by build_kp06_en.py and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp06.py.

p07-practice-q.name: p07-practice-q
p07-practice-q.text: (a) $M=4$, $l=5$: how many numbers do the concatenated $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf z_{ij}$ each have? (b) The sample is in class 1 with known $g_1=2.4,g_2=2.1,g_3=2.3$: write the known constraints and decide whether they hold. (c) Can we be sure it is classified correctly?

p07-practice-a1.name: p07-practice-a1
p07-practice-a1.text: (a) Each block has $l+1=6$ numbers, so $M(l+1)=4\times6=24$ numbers in all ($\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf z_{ij}$ have the same length).

p07-practice-a3.name: p07-practice-a3
p07-practice-a3.text: (c) Not yet. Class 4's score $g_4$ is not given, so the constraint $g_1-g_4>0$ is still missing. It must be compared with all $M-1=3$ rivals to count as the highest score.

p07-practice-a4.name: p07-practice-a4
p07-practice-a4.text: Comparing only two is not enough: as in the contrast on page 2, beating two can still lose to the third.

p08-summary-title.name: p08-summary-title
p08-summary-title.text: Summary: multiclass = beat every rival; Kesler writes it as the same kind of positive inner product

p08-summary-ctx.name: p08-summary-ctx
p08-summary-ctx.text: Recall along the three highest-score regions; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p08-summary-e0.name: p08-summary-e0
p08-summary-e0.text: Highest score = beat every rival at once: $g_i>g_j$ for all $j\ne i$ (a tie does not count as a win in training)

p08-summary-e1.name: p08-summary-e1
p08-summary-e1.text: Kesler: $\mathbf v=(\mathbf w_1,\dots,\mathbf w_M)$, $\mathbf z_{ij}=(\ldots,+\mathbf a,\ldots,-\mathbf a,\ldots)$, $\mathbf v^T\mathbf z_{ij}=g_i-g_j$

p08-summary-e2.name: p08-summary-e2
p08-summary-e2.text: $N(M-1)$ vectors in all, each of length $M(l+1)$; on a violation $\mathbf v\leftarrow\mathbf v+\rho\mathbf z_{ij}$ (correct class rises, rival falls)

p08-summary-e3.name: p08-summary-e3
p08-summary-e3.text: Only an equivalent rewriting: it neither solves non-separability nor equals one-versus-rest; adding the same vector does not change differences, the solution is not unique

p08-summary-e4.name: p08-summary-e4
p08-summary-e4.text: Open question: when data overlap (non-separable), do not demand a perfect fit; ask how close the outputs can get to the targets. Next KP: MSE
